newsitem.title: UK: UK rate rise not last before election - analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK rate rise not last before election - analysts.

text.p: A shock increase in UK interest rates on Wednesday left financial markets reeling and expecting further monetary tightening before elections.
They said Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's decision to raise base rates to 6.0 percent from 5.75 added to his credibility as a finance minister.

"Clarke has now demonstrated he is prepared to raise rates in the face of political flak so you have got to expect one and maybe two more moves before the election," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.

The Conservative government must call elections by May 1997 and trails badly in the opinion polls. More expensive borrowing costs, particularly for homeowners, will not be welcomed by Conservative politicians.

Shepperd said rates were raised presumably to stem inflationary pressures in the pipeline, heralded by rapid growth in consumer spending. "A quarter-point move will not in itself halt inflationary pressure," he said.
Bank of England Eddie George said in a statement that he welcomed Clarke's decision to raise rates and said a move now would moderate economic acceleration.
George said policy may now be tightened less stringently than would have been the case. "That statement seems to be hinting that further rate rises are in prospect," Shepperd said.
He said Clarke had taken another step to winning his spurs as a finance minister of prudence and responsibility.
The short sterling strip is discounting interest rates at about seven percent by the end of next year. "That's probably not too far from the truth," Shepperd said.
In a statement, Clarke said the UK economy was performing exceptionally well and he was determined to maintain a firm grip on inflation to sustain that growth well into the future.
"We must take no risks with inflation now or in the future," Clarke said.
Jeremy Peat, chief economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland, said the weight of economic evidence had move in favour of a rate rise.
"The Chancellor was in danger of both missing his inflation target and losing some hard won credibility," he said on Reuters Financial Television. "This move helps on both counts."
Analysts said Wednesday's rate rise would keep George off the Chancellor's back for now. But they said George would be sure to call for higher rates still before the election.
"Another quarter-point rate rise is still coming, probably in the first quarter (of 1997)," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

He said it was too early to say that Clarke would meet his underlying inflation target next year. "But he is obviously committed to sound economic management. The days of slash and burn economics are long gone."

Neither does the shock rate rise give Clarke more room to cut taxes in his November 26 budget. "A loose budget would not go down well with the electorate. Everyone knows public finances are not what they should be," Barr said.
He forecast tax cuts of around three billion stg, offset by planned spending cuts.

But if nothing else, Clarke has bought himself some breathing space. Barr said the Bank of England's quarterly inflation report, due next Wednesday, would probably have taken an aggressive line on monetary policy.

Gilts and short sterling futures dived after the rate cut but analysts said the long end of the market could soon pick up as fears of rampant inflation ease and in grudging admiration of Clarke's move. "It's Chancellor one, city nil," Jeremy Hawkins, economist at BankAmerica said on Shy TV.
